title: Add Binary
description: Brute force to optimized: integer conversion versus digit-by-digit addition with a running carry, safe for input of any length.

blocks.text: Given two binary strings a and b, return their sum, also as a binary string.

blocks.title: Analogy: Grade School Addition, Just With Two Digits Instead of Ten
blocks.text: This is exactly the column by column addition learned in school, lining up two numbers by their rightmost digit and carrying into the next column whenever a column adds up to more than the base allows. The only difference here is that each column can only hold a 0 or a 1, so anything of value 2 or more immediately carries over.

blocks.caption: Add two binary strings column by column, carrying between columns

blocks.text: Both inputs are zero, so the sum is simply "0".
Converting both strings to a number and adding them feels like the obvious approach, so it is worth checking exactly what that approach is quietly assuming.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Converting each binary string to an integer, adding, and converting back gives the right answer, but only as long as the language's integer type is wide enough to hold the full value both inputs represent.

Observation 2: Since the input strings can be up to 10000 characters long, the numeric value they represent can be astronomically larger than any native fixed width integer type could ever hold, so this assumption quietly fails for large enough input.

Observation 3: Grade school column addition never actually needs the full numeric value at once, it only ever needs the two digits in the current column plus whatever carried in from the column before it.

Observation 4: Applying that same column by column process directly to the two strings, from their rightmost characters inward, with an explicit carry variable, reproduces the correct sum without ever assuming any fixed width integer type is large enough.

That observation, that a native integer conversion silently assumes a size limit the problem does not actually guarantee, is exactly why this problem is normally asked as a digit by digit addition exercise, not an integer conversion exercise.
Convert each binary string into an ordinary integer, add the two integers together using normal arithmetic, then convert that sum back into a binary string.

items: Parse the first binary string into an integer.
Parse the second binary string into an integer.
Add the two integers together.
Convert the resulting sum back into its binary string representation.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: convert both strings to integers, add, then convert back

codes.python:
def add_binary(a, b):
    x = int(a, 2)                              # convert the first binary string to an integer
    y = int(b, 2)                               # convert the second binary string to an integer
    return bin(x + y)[2:]                       # add them, then strip the leading "0b" marker


if __name__ == "__main__":
    a, b = "11", "1"
    print(add_binary(a, b))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Both strings are parsed using a built in base-2 parser, letting the language handle the digit weighting instead of writing that conversion by hand.
The addition itself is a single native operation, relying entirely on the language's own integer arithmetic to produce the correct sum.
Converting the sum back to a binary string reuses another built in formatter, keeping this version as short as possible, at the cost of depending on the integer type underneath it.

blocks.text: This is correct, since converting to an integer, adding, and converting back preserves the exact numeric value throughout.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), where n is the length of the longer string, for the two conversions and the final formatting.
Space: O(n), for the resulting string.

Limitation: this approach quietly depends on the language being able to hold a number as large as the input represents. Binary addition problems like this one are commonly used to test whether digit by digit addition can be done directly on the strings, the same way addition is done by hand, without ever needing to hold the full numeric value in a single variable.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the integer conversion version works for small inputs but is not truly general: it depends entirely on the language's integer type being wide enough, an assumption that silently breaks once the input strings get long enough.

What grade school column addition actually needs at each step: just the two current digits and the carry from the previous column, never the full accumulated value.

Can that column by column process be applied directly to the two strings: yes, starting from the rightmost character of each and moving inward, exactly mirrors how addition is done by hand.

What happens once one string runs out of digits: the carry, and any remaining digits from the longer string, keep being processed exactly as before, simply treating the exhausted string as contributing 0 from then on.

The core idea: walk both strings from right to left, adding the current digits plus the carry, keeping the last bit of that sum as the output digit and the rest as the new carry, continuing until both strings and the carry are exhausted.

Walk both strings from their last character toward the first, adding the two digits at the current position along with any carry from the previous column. The last bit of that sum is the digit for this column, and the rest carries into the next one. Continue until both strings, and any final carry, are exhausted.
Add the two binary strings column by column from the right, tracking a running carry, and continue until both strings and the carry are fully exhausted.
Reading the placed digits from last to first gives "100".

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: add digit by digit from the right, carrying into the next column

blocks.text: This works because binary addition, like any positional addition, is entirely defined by adding two digits plus an incoming carry at each column, producing an outgoing digit and a new carry, exactly the loop implemented here. Once one string is exhausted, its contribution to every remaining column is simply 0, which the loop reflects naturally by only adding a digit from a string that still has characters left; the loop only stops once both strings AND the carry are simultaneously exhausted, correctly capturing a final leftover carry as one more leading digit.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), the same order as the brute force, where n is the length of the longer string.
Space: O(n), for the result string, this is the real floor for this problem, since a result of that length must always be produced, but no big integer conversion is ever needed, so it stays safe no matter how long the input strings are.

blocks.text: This is the classic digit by digit addition pattern, the same idea used whenever numbers are represented as strings or linked lists rather than native integers, since it never assumes the full value can fit in a single variable. Track a running carry, process from the least significant end, and stop once both inputs and the carry are exhausted.

items: Forgetting to keep processing after one string runs out of digits, the carry and the remaining string still need to be handled.
Forgetting a final carry that is left over after both strings are fully consumed.
Building the result in the wrong order and forgetting to reverse it at the end.

blocks.text: Explicitly mentioning that converting to a native integer is unsafe for arbitrarily long input strings, and that the expected approach processes digit by digit with a carry, shows an understanding of exactly why this problem is usually asked in the first place.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "what if the input is too large for a native integer", think: process digit by digit with a running carry, exactly like grade school column addition.
If the interviewer says "what happens when the strings have different lengths", think: keep going once a string is exhausted, treating its missing digits as 0, until the carry runs out too.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid reversing the result at the end", think: prepend each digit instead of appending it, at the cost of a less efficient string operation in some languages.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches run in O(n) time, where n is the length of the longer string. The integer conversion approach uses O(n) space but depends on the language supporting numbers as large as the input represents. The digit by digit approach also uses O(n) space, the real floor for this problem, and stays safe for input of any length.

items: Pattern: digit by digit addition with a running carry, processed from the least significant end, the same technique used whenever numbers are represented as strings or linked lists instead of native integers.

Core Idea: grade school column addition never needs the full numeric value at once, only the current digits and the incoming carry, so walking both strings from right to left with an explicit carry variable reproduces the correct sum regardless of input length.
Time: O(n) for both the brute force and the optimized version, where n is the length of the longer string.
Space: O(n) for both versions, to hold the resulting string.
Most Important Observation: converting to a native integer silently assumes a size limit the problem may not actually guarantee; digit by digit processing with a carry makes no such assumption.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write the integer conversion version; recognizing and explaining why it is not truly general is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: add right to left, digit plus digit plus carry, keep the last bit, carry the rest.
